Apache Arrow · WebAssembly components · Rust · Go · Python · TypeScript · Kotlin · C#

Batch pipelines that
work out their own order

PCS is a columnar batch processing engine for Rust, built on Apache Arrow. You write transforms in Rust, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, or C# and say which columns each one reads and writes. PCS derives the execution plan, runs independent work concurrently, and loads the whole pipeline as a WebAssembly component.

Install and run in 15 minutes Write a WebAssembly processor
License AGPL-3.0-only Rust 1.95+ Status experimental

Where the name comes from

PCS is Pipeline Component System, a nod to ECS, the Entity Component System pattern from game development. ECS organises game entities as components that systems act on each frame. PCS keeps the Component and the System and swaps the entity for a data Pipeline, so a frame of entities becomes a batch of Arrow columns. The field declarations come from there too: an ECS scheduler groups systems by the components each one names, and PCS does the same one level finer, per field.

Two ways to run a pipeline

The pipeline code is the same either way. The choice is deployment: the transform ships inside your binary or as a file the host loads.

WASM Processors

You ship a .wasm

pcs-service loads it at startup, in any language that targets WASI 0.2. Change the pipeline without rebuilding the host.

 Native

Your binary links the engine

You own main and call pipeline.run(). No wasmtime, no service, and a debugger on the same process.

The idea in one diagram

You never write a stage list. Each system declares the fields it touches, and PCS derives what can run together.

Why columns

Storing each field as a contiguous Arrow column, instead of a row per record, changes what the machine has to move.

▮

Read only what you touch

A system reading 3 of 50 columns loads 24 MB instead of 400 MB per million rows. The rest never enters cache.

⇄

Handoff is a pointer

Passing a batch between stages is an Arc clone: one atomic increment, no buffer copy.

◇

Checkpoints are a memcpy

Arrow IPC writes contiguous buffers, so crash recovery decodes 6× faster than a row-oriented equivalent at 1M rows.

See the benchmark numbers and how they were measured

Is PCS a fit?

Reach for PCS when
  • Work arrives as batches of 100k to 100M rows, or as a stream of individual items
  • The transform is imperative Rust that SQL expresses awkwardly
  • Schemas are wide: tens to hundreds of columns, and each step reads a few
  • You need recovery time to be a design constraint, not an afterthought
Look elsewhere when
  • You want SQL. There is no query planner here; DataFusion will win
  • You need hard real-time guarantees. Stream mode is sub-millisecond per item in-process, but it is not a real-time scheduler
  • You are building a game engine. The ECS vocabulary is a naming nod, nothing more
  • Your data is under ~10k rows. A plain Vec will beat this

Five concepts, in order

Each one builds on the previous, so nothing is forward-referenced. All five apply to both modes, because a processor runs the same Pipeline DAG inside the component. The sixth card is that boundary itself.

01

Dataset

The columnar container. One Arrow RecordBatch per registered Component, all sharing a row count.
02

System

One transform, plus the meta() that names which columns it reads and writes.
03

Pipeline

A Dataset and its Systems. Turns declarations into stages, and retries what fails.
04

Scheduler

Several independent Pipelines in one process, with dependency edges between them.
05

Distributed processing

The same Pipeline against claimed row ranges across nodes, with claims and checkpoints replicated by raft.
+

WASM Processors

The contract is a WIT world, not an SDK. A recipe per language, and a worked example chaining six processors in Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, C#, and Rust over one schema.

How a pipeline ships

This is the WebAssembly processor path. You do not deploy a binary containing your pipeline; you deploy pcs-service once and hand it components. A native pipeline skips all of this and ships as your own binary.

Prior art

Conduit is the strongest influence on this project. It streams data between stores in Go, builds a pipeline from source and destination connectors plus processors, keeps the plugin contract language-agnostic so a connector can be written in anything, runs standalone processors as WebAssembly, and either embeds in your own binary or runs as a service you hand a config to. Every one of those shapes is here, with a WIT world in place of the gRPC interface.

The unit of work is what differs. A Conduit pipeline carries records; a PCS pipeline carries Arrow batches, and works out its execution order from the columns each system declares.

Where this project is

PCS explores two questions: how far specialised coding agents can maintain a non-trivial multi-crate Rust codebase, and what a Rust-native batch engine with WebAssembly extensibility should look like. It is not production-ready, and the crates are not published to crates.io. Feedback and contributions are welcome.
